hero.title: A machine that learned to write like Dostoevsky
hero.lead: In 2020, Google researchers trained a language model on Crime and Punishment. This museum tells that story and lets you try it live.

novel.title: Crime and Punishment, 1866
novel.lead: Long before artificial intelligence, there was this novel: the story of Raskolnikov, a student in Saint Petersburg wrestling with guilt, poverty, and redemption.
novel.cardBody: Fyodor Dostoevsky published Crime and Punishment in 1866. More than a century later, a Google team used the English text of the novel — now in the public domain — to teach a machine to mimic its rhythm and tone. It is not a summary or a translation: it is an experiment asking whether a book can teach a style.

1866.title: Crime and Punishment is published
1866.description: Dostoevsky finishes one of the nineteenth century's most influential novels. The text outlives generations and eventually reaches public-domain digital libraries.

2020-paper.title: Google introduces Reformer
2020-paper.description: Researchers publish Reformer: The Efficient Transformer, an architecture built to handle long sequences with less memory than classic transformers.

2020-trained.title: Trained on the novel
2020-trained.description: Google trains a Reformer checkpoint on English passages from Crime and Punishment — roughly half a million words — and releases it as google/reformer-crime-and-punishment.

today.title: You can try it yourself
today.description: This museum loads that same 2020 model in the cloud. Type a few words and watch how it continues the text with Dostoevsky's echo.

read.title: It read the book
read.description: The model was exposed to the full English text of Crime and Punishment, word by word, many times over.

patterns.title: It learned patterns
patterns.description: Without understanding the plot like a human, it picked up how sentences tend to chain together: the rhythm, the pauses, and the words Dostoevsky repeats.

continue.title: It continues your sentences
continue.description: You write the start of a sentence; the model suggests words that might follow, as if finishing a paragraph from the book.

footer.author: jseramn
footer.tagline: An open museum about one of the earliest Reformer language models — for learning history, not replacing reading.
footer.privacyNote: PostHog records page views and usage events anonymously. We do not store the text you type.

experiment.title: Try the model
experiment.description: Write an opening line and let the 2020 Reformer model continue the passage in the style of Crime and Punishment.
experiment.promptPlaceholder: Write the opening of a passage…
experiment.expectationWarning: The output may sound strange or incoherent — that is expected for a small 2020 research model.
experiment.englishNote: Note: the model writes in English.
experiment.playgroundEmpty: Write a prompt or use a suggested opening to start the chat.
